name: Maldahar the Glimmer Prince

facts.text: A level-73 named with 40,000 health who roams the Sheeroe Hills (388276, 696824).
He cannot be crowd-controlled (CCImmunity) and resets to full after 60 seconds out of combat.
Bot chat calls him the Glimmer King's son and warns that counting glimmers aloud brings him.
The father-son tie is Living Server lore: no Mythic source names his parentage.
Colm, Eoghan's wife, the Ardee six and the Lough Gur visits in his chapters are Living Server lore.

story:
Maldahar the Glimmer Prince appeared the spring after the sky tore over Sheeroe, riding the prince's road below his father's lair on a horse of cold light, and the Glimmer parted for him. The name came from the Azure, who say they heard the light call him so. Whether he is Cuuldurach's son by blood the bards still argue; the shepherds settled it for themselves by the way he looks back toward the lair when he rides.

His duty is the borders. The rule about never counting the glimmers aloud dates from his first season, when a herder's boy named Colm counted a camp for a wager and the prince came down within the minute. A band of six from Ardee learned the first fact about him: no mesmerism, root or stun has ever held him, because, the druids say, he is not wholly on this side of the Veil. A stronger band learned the second: leave him alone for a minute and he is whole again. So he is fought by strong groups, with no tricks and no pause, well away from the glimmer camps.

He rides further than his father's court, as far as Lough Gur, where the Melancholic Fairy Queen weeps beside a shut door; whether he courts her, scouts her, or is only lonely, the realm keeps all three accounts. When he falls every glimmer on the ridge dims for a breath and the king turns his head, and the veterans leave the ridge quickly. Like his father he returns. The Azure, who fight every other light on Sheeroe, are forbidden by their leader Dsaldor to raise a hand against him, though they have burned his father's courtiers for years, and will not say why; Coseal their preacher says only that the son is not the father.
legend: Mezz and root are wasted on him, so bring damage, not tricks. Commit to the fight: if your group drifts off for a minute he heals to full and you start again. Pull him away from the glimmer camps so the court does not join. And never count the glimmers aloud on the ridge, or so every Sheeroe veteran swears. He is a group's target, not a raid's: a strong group with no tricks can do it if it commits and does not stop. Pull him well away from the glimmer camps. Superstition: never call him by name on the ridge, call him 'the rider', or he hears you and comes. The shepherds say he dims the ridge when he dies, and that you should not be standing on the ridge when the king notices.

loremasterTopic.text: The Glimmer Prince, who rides the borders of his father's court. No charm holds him, and if he is let be for a minute he is whole again. Fight him all at once or not at all.

bookPage: From Eoghan the shepherd's account: the rider goes further than his father's court. I have seen him at the edge of the bog in winter, sitting his horse of light and looking west, toward Lough Gur, where the sad queen of the Good Folk weeps beside her shut door. Some say he courts her. My wife says he is lonely, which is a woman's answer and may be the true one. The raids that go after him say no charm holds him and no sleep takes him, and if they let him be for a minute he is whole again. Princes are like that, my wife says. They do not keep their wounds. Other people keep them for them.

chapters.title: The Heir
chapters.text:
Maldahar was not seen the summer the sky tore. Eoghan's grandmother, who watched the wings come through, saw only the king and the lights. The prince appeared the following spring, riding down the prince's road below the lair on a horse of cold light, and the shepherds understood at once what he was from the way the Glimmer parted for him. The realm named him the Glimmer Prince, and the name Maldahar came from the Azure, who claimed to have heard the light call him so.

Whether he is the king's son by blood, nobody can prove. The bards of Tir na Nog argued it for a season in the taverns: a king and a prince make a father and a son, said one side; a prince only proves a royal house, said the other, and queens have princes too. Brónach of Lough Gur ended the argument for most Hibernians by pointing out that he looks back toward the lair over his shoulder when he rides, the way a son looks back at a father's house. The bards still argue. The shepherds do not.

His duty is the borders. Where the court attends, the prince patrols, along the ridge, down to the head of the pass, and back. The shepherds' rule about never counting the glimmers aloud dates from his first season: a herder's boy named Colm counted a camp of them for a wager, and the prince came down the ridge within the minute and looked at him, and Colm did not speak for a week.

chapters.title: No Charm Holds Him
chapters.text:
The first band to try him was a group of six from Ardee who thought a prince would be easier than a king. Their enchanter laid a mesmerism on him; it slid off like water off oilcloth. Their druid rooted him; the roots found nothing to hold. Their warrior struck to stun; the prince did not notice. That is the origin of the one fact every Hibernian knows about him, told by the two of the six who came home: no charm, sleep or binding has ever taken hold of Maldahar. The druids of Lough Gur say he is not wholly on this side of the Veil, and that you cannot hold what is only partly here.

The second fact was learned by a stronger band the next month, and it is crueller. They fought him for half the afternoon and drove him to near his last, and then their healers called a halt to mend, and they drew back for the space of a long breath. When they came again he was whole. A prince does not keep his wounds, Eoghan's wife said when she heard; other people keep them for him. The realm's raid leaders say it more plainly: leave him alone for a minute and you start again.

So the realm fights him as it fights nothing else on Sheeroe: a strong group, no tricks, and no pause. He is a group's quarry, not a raid's. The veterans pull him well away from the glimmer camps first, because the court comes to its prince as it comes to its king.

chapters.title: The Rider at Lough Gur
chapters.text:
The prince goes further than his father's court ever reaches. Eoghan saw him in winter at the very edge of the Bog of Cullen, sitting his horse of light and looking west. West of the bog lies Lough Gur, and at Lough Gur, after dark, a fairy queen of the bright court weeps beside a door into the hill that has not opened for her since the night the courts quarrelled in the Cursed Forest. Some nights, the Ardee folk say, the prince rides as far as the lake and watches her across the water. He never goes nearer.

There are three explanations and the realm keeps all of them. The bards say he courts her, a prince of the far side and a queen locked out of her own, and that the trumpets that sound when she comes are for him. The druids say he is a scout, and that the far side is looking for every place where the Veil is thin, and that a weeping queen by a shut door marks one. Eoghan's wife says he is lonely, which the bards call a woman's answer, and which Brónach of Lough Gur says may be the true one.

What all the accounts agree on is that he never stays. Before dawn he is back on the ridge above Sheeroe, riding the borders, and the Glimmer part for him again. The trumpets at Lough Gur, the Ardee folk add, sound differently on the nights he has been watching: lower, and shorter, as if whoever plays them were listening for something across the water. Nobody in Ardee has ever been willing to sit by the lake long enough to be sure.

chapters.title: When the Prince Falls
chapters.text:
When the realm's groups bring him down, every glimmer on the ridge dims at once, for the space of a breath, as a hall falls silent when the heir is carried out. The shepherds noticed it first; the realm's fighters, busy with the kill, noticed it later, and now watch for it. And somewhere at the top of the hills something very large turns its head. No raid has ever been attacked by the king for killing his son. But the veterans of Sheeroe have a rule: when the prince is down, do not stand on the ridge. Go down the pass, quickly, and let the king grieve in private.

Like his father he returns. The Azure take this as proof that neither is truly alive; the druids take it as proof that the door behind them is open. Either way the prince's road is never empty for long, and the shepherds' children are still told the rule about counting. The scribes of Tir na Nog note a last detail from Colm, the boy who counted the camp: years later, grown and a fighter of the realm, he rode with a group that brought the prince down. He said the prince looked at him exactly as he had the first time, as though he remembered. Colm swore he would never count anything in Sheeroe again, not even his own coin, and as far as anyone knows he never did.

The Azure have their own rule about the prince. Dsaldor, who leads their crusade, forbids his people to fight him at all, and the realm has never learned why. Coseal the preacher says only that the son is not the father, and that the Order's quarrel is with the king and the light he stole.
